title: NYC Unclaimed Money: Search and Claim Guide (October 2026)
summary: Learn the steps to search New York's unclaimed funds database and claim a deceased person's money, updated for October 2026.
body_markdown:
The New York State Comptroller’s Office of Unclaimed Funds holds money that banks, insurers, and other businesses have turned over to the state, including money owed to a person who has died. Whether a family member can claim that money depends on who has legal authority over the deceased person’s estate. This guide covers key points for families and executors, including: how to search the state database, who is authorized to claim funds, what documents a claim requires, how to file a claim, where other unclaimed money may be held, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- New York's free state search uses the deceased person's last name, not the claimant's.
- If an estate representative was appointed, that person may claim the funds.
- Claims require proof of ownership, legal entitlement, and the owner's death.
- After approval, New York generally mails the claim check within 30 days.
- Elayne's Verified Asset Search looks beyond state registries for accounts, insurance, and benefits.


## What Unclaimed Funds Are and Why They Exist


Unclaimed funds are money or financial assets left inactive or uncollected, such as old bank accounts and uncashed checks. After a period of inactivity, businesses transfer qualifying assets to the state for safekeeping through the unclaimed property program.


A deceased person's unclaimed money may be held by New York State. Before releasing it, the state uses a formal claim process to verify ownership and the claimant's right to receive the funds.

## New York's Abandoned Property Law


New York's Abandoned Property Law requires banks, insurers, utilities, and corporations to report and remit funds that meet abandonment criteria to the State Comptroller's Office of Unclaimed Funds.


Most property types have a three-year dormancy threshold, though timing varies by asset type. Dormancy is a legally defined period without qualifying owner activity or contact. After that period, institutions must follow reporting and transfer requirements instead of holding the money indefinitely.


## The Two Distinct Unclaimed Funds Programs in New York


For unclaimed funds in NYC, a strong starting point is the statewide database.


Office Relevant funds


New York State Comptroller's Office of Unclaimed Funds[Dormant bank accounts](https://www.elayne.com/resources/decedent-bank-account-search-guide) , insurance proceeds, and stocks


New York City Comptroller Certain city payments, including unclaimed warrants (uncashed city-issued checks)


The NYC Comptroller's city claims process handles claims against or on behalf of the city, separate from the state's unclaimed-property search.


## How to Search for a Deceased Person's Unclaimed Funds in New York


The[State Comptroller's search database](https://ouf.osc.ny.gov/app/claim-search) offers a free search for unclaimed funds in New York. Key points to note:


1. Searches use the deceased person's last name.
2. First name, city, and ZIP code help narrow results.
3. Former names and previous residences can reveal other matches.


According to the State Comptroller’s[guidance for deceased-owner claims](https://www.osc.ny.gov/unclaimed-funds/claimants/claims-deceased-owners-and-estates) , listed property minimum values are $20 or one share of stock. The office discloses the value after reviewing the claim.


## Who Has the Authority to Claim a Deceased Person's Unclaimed Funds


The Surrogate's Court in the deceased person's home county handles estate matters. If an estate representative was appointed, that representative may claim unclaimed funds. For context:


- An executor is named in the will; court-issued Letters Testamentary document their authority.
- An administrator is court-appointed when there is no will; Letters of Administration document their authority.


## What Documentation Is Required to Claim Funds for a Deceased Owner


A deceased-owner unclaimed funds claim requires three kinds of proof:


- Ownership: bank statements, insurance policies, or stock certificates connecting the deceased person to the funds.
- Entitlement: documents showing the claimant’s legal right to claim, such as Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration. Some small-estate claims may require an Affidavit of Heirship; requirements depend on the estate.
- Death: a death certificate copy, certified if required by the claim instructions.


## How to File a Claim for a Deceased Person's Unclaimed Funds


Online filing for a deceased person’s unclaimed funds begins by selecting “Claim” beside a matching property, then “Continue to File Claim.” Mail submissions include the completed claim form and supporting copies, sent according to the form’s instructions.


After approval, the check is generally mailed within 30 days. The online claim status tool uses the Claim ID from the confirmation email. Restrictions on disclosing property values help prevent fraud.


## Federal and Other Sources of Unclaimed Funds to Search


Resources include:


- MissingMoney.com, a NAUPA-endorsed multistate database.
- TreasuryDirect for matured savings bonds.
- Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) for[unclaimed retirement benefits](https://www.elayne.com/resources/find-lost-retirement-accounts) .
- Department of Labor for unpaid wages.
- IRS for unclaimed tax refunds.


The deceased person’s former residences and employment records can help guide these searches.


## How Unclaimed Funds Fit Into the Broader Estate Settlement Picture


State unclaimed funds databases list assets already reported and transferred to the state. Other accounts may remain at their original institutions until they have been inactive long enough to meet transfer rules.


A broader estate search includes[bank and investment accounts](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-find-all-bank-and-investment-accounts-after-someone-dies) still held by those institutions, forgotten life insurance policies, and potential unpaid survivor benefits through Social Security, the VA, or pensions. These sources require searches beyond state databases, which a[complete guide to finding deceased accounts](https://www.elayne.com/resources/complete-guide-finding-deceased-loved-one-accounts) can help clarify.

## How Elayne Supports Unclaimed Asset Discovery After a Death


State unclaimed funds databases list property that has already been reported and transferred to the state. Other accounts, policies, and benefits can remain at their original institutions, sit with government programs, or appear only in records that a family has not yet reviewed. Elayne’s Verified Asset Search covers these additional sources alongside state unclaimed property registries.


State searches and Elayne’s search draw on different sources. The New York State Comptroller’s database lists property already transferred to the state, while Verified Asset Search also covers life insurance records, credit bureau data, property and vehicle records, and clues in a family’s own financial documents.


Verified Asset Search looks for several types of assets and records. These include real property and deeds, vehicle and vessel records, and life insurance policies through the NAIC life insurance locator. They also include unclaimed and state-held property, such as savings bonds and PBGC benefits. Credit bureau trade-line searches across Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion can help locate debts, and recurring payments can point to accounts and subscriptions that continue to bill after a death.


Elayne also analyzes documents that families already have, such as tax returns, bank statements, and other financial records. Interest payments, retirement distributions, and dividend income listed in those documents point to institutions that may hold estate assets.


Survivor benefits are part of the search as well. Elayne identifies which Social Security, pension, veterans’, and union benefits may apply to an estate, along with the eligibility requirements and deadlines attached to each one.


Elayne scans financial records for recurring charges, such as streaming services, gym memberships, and software. Cancellation is managed directly with each provider, later statements are monitored to confirm the charges stopped, and each confirmation is logged for estate accounting.


Search results are organized into one structured estate record. Authorized family members, executors, advisors, and attorneys view that record through a shared dashboard with role-based permissions.


Verified Asset Search is part of Elayne’s Financial Discovery tier. Elayne is an eligible estate expense. When a confirmed estate account exists, Elayne can bill the estate directly; otherwise, the cost can be reimbursed from estate funds once authority and the account are in place.


In short, these searches work in layers: the state database lists property already transferred, Verified Asset Search covers accounts, insurance, property, and benefits held elsewhere, and the person with legal authority over the estate makes any claim that follows.


## FAQ


### Can someone search the New York State Comptroller’s database before being appointed executor?


Yes, the free public unclaimed funds search is separate from the process of proving a claimant’s authority to claim. Possible matches can be recorded while estate paperwork is pending, but a search result does not give the searcher the legal right to receive the money.


### Can Elayne’s Verified Asset Search help when a New York unclaimed funds search finds nothing?


A broader search can help if financial records suggest accounts or insurance policies that the state database does not list. A no-match result does not rule out assets still held by banks or insurers; Elayne’s Verified Asset Search reviews financial records and other sources for those assets and eligible benefits.


### How does a New York State Comptroller unclaimed funds claim proceed if the deceased person’s bank statements are missing?


The Office of Unclaimed Funds can clarify which other ownership records it will accept for a claim. The claim instructions determine the required proof, so confirming acceptable alternatives before submitting can help avoid an incomplete application.


### Who can claim a deceased person’s unclaimed funds in New York when no estate representative has been appointed?


The Comptroller’s office allows a limited group of family members to claim in this situation. The closest living family member may submit a claim with a copy of the death certificate, a completed Small Estates Affidavit, and a completed Table of Heirs. Eligible family members are limited to the following, in order:


- A spouse.
- Biological or legally adopted children, if there is no surviving spouse.
- Parents, if there is no surviving spouse or children.
- Siblings, if there is no surviving spouse, children, or parents.


If the value of the funds is less than $1,000, the office may process the claim, and the payee must distribute the funds under New York’s intestacy laws. If the funds are worth $1,000 or more, only a court-appointed representative may complete the claim. If none of the listed family members is living, only a court-appointed representative may submit a claim. These rules appear in the[Comptroller’s deceased-owner claim rules](https://www.osc.ny.gov/unclaimed-funds/claimants/claims-deceased-owners-and-estates) .
